title: When work ends
hookLine: putting work down at the end of the day
tomorrow: on this path, is it okay to want money?

lines: OFF AT SIX. STILL AT IT AT NINE.
cards: The shift ends at six. At nine, you're still answering a customer in your head who left hours ago. The body clocked out; the mind took the work home on its back.
So how do you stop carrying it? The Buddha tells a story about a man who almost did exactly that, with a raft.

teach.h: A RAFT OF GRASS AND STICKS.
teach.b: A man comes to a wide river. No boat, no bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet.
On the far shore he thinks: this raft was so useful. I'll lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go. Would that be the right thing to do with a raft? the Buddha asks.

teach.h: ON THE FAR SHORE: SET IT DOWN.
teach.b: Set it down on the shore, or let it float, and go on. In the sutta, the raft is the teaching itself: for crossing over, not for holding on to. Bringing it to a workday is a stretch, and an honest one.
The work got you across the day. Thank it and set it down. A neighbor tradition says something close, in a different voice.

teach.h: MATTHEW: I WILL GIVE YOU REST.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." That's what they share: the weight of work is real, and it isn't meant to ride on you forever.
In Matthew, rest is given: Christians hear Jesus offering it to whoever comes. In the raft story, nobody hands rest over.
The one who crossed sees the raft has done its job, and sets it down. A gift received; a load released.

how: Buddhist teachers use the raft simile to warn against clinging, even to the teaching, and some lay practitioners mark the end of a workday with a short sit or a few quiet breaths.

o: setting work down once it has done its job
quitting a job as soon as it gets hard
working until every task is finished

games.q: the raft and the rest — tap the pairs.
p: set it down and go on
rest offered to the heavy laden

s: the raft simile says to cling tightly to the teaching
even the teaching is a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to.
in the story, the man thinks about carrying the raft on his head
it was so useful he wants to keep it; the Buddha says set it down.
Matthew 11:28 and the raft story say exactly the same thing
both ease the load; in Matthew rest is given, in the story the load is set down.

games.q: you got home an hour ago and you're still rewriting a message to your boss in your head. what would the man with the raft do?
o: thank the day for getting him across, and leave it on the shore.
keep it on his head; it was useful, so it might be again.
smash the raft in anger; it never should have been needed.
games.why: the raft was good; that's why he's tempted to carry it. the Buddha's answer: set it on the shore and go on.

practice: Close your eyes and rest your hands on your knees, closed gently, as if holding the day's work: the task, the email, the face. Then open your hands, palms up, and let it rest on the shore.
Each time it climbs back on, open them again.

wordCard.voice: When work ends: the moment to set the raft down. It got you across, and you don't carry it home on your head.

orig.note: Pali: kulla, a raft; MN 22's simile says the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to.

carryVoice: Your line: put it down. The raft has done its job for today. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft: for crossing over, not for grasping)

sources.q: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
